output.title: Rollback plans are not the real control
output.body:
Rollback plans sound tidy until you look at the actual workflow risk. In a small business, the real problem is usually not “can we undo it later?” It is “what happens while this automation is running?” If the wrong customer reply goes out, a duplicate invoice is created, or a manual step gets bypassed, rolling back after the fact does not erase the damage already in motion.

That is why rollback is not enough on its own. It restores the previous state. It does not stop bad data, bad answers, or bad decisions from propagating. For an owner, the better question is simple: which part of this process needs a gate before anything is committed?

Start with one repeatable workflow you are thinking about automating. Write down the three most damaging failure modes: wrong data, missed items, and duplicates. Then choose one human approval step that would block the worst one before it reaches payment, the inbox, or the CRM. If you are testing invoice extraction, for example, spot-check a few entries against the source documents before anything is posted. That is a control. A rollback plan is still useful, but it is the backup plan, not the main defense.

Bareni’s policy is that finished code is handed over and the accounts stay in the customer’s name from the start. That is no-lock-in positioning, not a legal warranty. The practical move is still the same: control the workflow first, then decide whether automation belongs there at all.
